items.title: What is meant by 'Second Urbanisation of India'?
items.explanation: The Second Urbanisation refers to the emergence of new vibrant urban centres in the Ganga plains, parts of the Indus/Sindhu basin, and neighbouring regions during the 1st millennium BCE. This phase replaced the disintegrated First Urbanisation (Indus/Harappan) with a system where clans formed under rulers called Rajas, leading to the creation of Janapadas and eventually Mahajanapadas.

items.title: Why were Janapadas and Mahajanapadas important in India's early history?
items.explanation: They were crucial because they represented a shift from loose tribal groups to organized political entities. The formation of these states allowed for the expansion of trade networks, the consolidation of power through assemblies (Sabhā/Samiti), and the establishment of administrative structures that supported productive economies with mines, forests, and waterways.

items.title: What kind of system of governance did they evolve?
items.explanation: They evolved into a system based on regional cultures where each Janapada had an assembly or council (Sabhā/Samiti) for discussing clan matters. The Rāja ruled under the advice of these assemblies and ministers, rather than ruling arbitrarily.
